paragraphs.heading: Rules for how planets move
paragraphs.text: Kepler's laws are the rules that describe the orbits of the planets. Johannes Kepler worked them out by joining his own ideas about physical causes with careful observations of the planets made by Tycho Brahe. His model treated each orbit as an ellipse. It made predictions of where the planets would be far more accurate than before.

paragraphs.heading: Two worlds brought together
paragraphs.text: Before Kepler, the people who predicted planet positions with geometry or numbers had little contact with the people who argued about what physically made the planets move. Kepler was the first to tie these two sides closely together. The geometric, prediction-first approach had ruled astronomy from Ptolemy in the 2nd century all the way to Copernicus. In 1609 Kepler set out his combined view in a book titled New Astronomy, Based upon Causes, or Celestial Physics.

paragraphs.heading: Newton explains why
paragraphs.text: Kepler's model came years before Isaac Newton worked out his law of gravitation in 1686. Newton introduced the idea that one set of physical laws covers both the sky and the ground, from planets and the Moon to falling apples and cannon balls. With his law of gravity he derived Kepler's laws for elliptical orbits from the two-body problem, the case of two objects pulling on each other by gravity. He published this in his Principia in 1687.

paragraphs.heading: Where the laws hold and bend
paragraphs.text: For a pair of objects held together by gravity, Newton's mechanics yields a set of orbital elements that predict where both will be with reasonable accuracy. This method shows that Kepler's laws are correct. When one of the two bodies is massive enough, though, general relativity has to be added to predict apsidal precession. Adding a third body makes things harder still, giving a three-body problem that has no exact solution.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond the ellipse
paragraphs.text: Later, Joseph-Louis Lagrange restated the principles of classical mechanics, putting more weight on energy than on force. He found a way to describe any orbit with a single equation in polar coordinates, including parabolic and hyperbolic ones. Those shapes are conic section extensions of Kepler's elliptical orbits, and they help in working out how planets and comets behave. In more recent times the same approach has also been used to plan the paths of spacecraft.
